question: Captain James Cook took several tonnes of one fermented food on his voyages to keep his sailors from getting scurvy. What was it?
source_excerpt: proper Quantities of sauer Kraut and Rob

extra.why_interesting: Players picture sailors and scurvy and think of lemons and limes. The surprise is that a famous British navigator relied on a German fermented cabbage, and had to coax his crew into eating it.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources confirm Cook carried multi-ton quantities of sauerkraut on his voyages against scurvy (https://hekint.org/2021/06/17/plague-of-the-sea-and-the-spoyle-of-mariners-a-brief-history-of-fermented-cabbage-as-antiscorbutic/).

explanation: Fermented cabbage keeps for months at sea and still has some vitamin C. Cook got his reluctant crew to eat it by serving it at the officers' table first, so the sailors decided it must be a treat.

question: When posing for a photo, English speakers say 'cheese' to force a smile. In South Korea, people often say the name of a different food instead. Which one?
source_excerpt: kimchi serves as South Korea's version of "cheese" for drawing smiles during photographs.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume 'say cheese' is a universal photo habit. Learning that Koreans swap in their national fermented dish for the same smile-shaping reason is a charming surprise, and the pack's theme gives a clear path to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: AP reporting confirms kimchi is South Korea's photo-smile word equivalent to 'cheese'; no newer development contradicts it (https://www.staradvertiser.com/2012/03/28/breaking-news/kimchi-tops-cheese-at-nuclear-summit/).

explanation: Both words end in the same 'ee' sound, which stretches the lips into a grin. So Korea's favourite fermented cabbage doubles as a camera cue.
